Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
• The liver metastases have shown a partial radiologic response (three lesions disappeared, the remaining lesions reduced by ~40 % and are now hypo‑intense on MRI) – a favorable sign that conversion to resection may be possible.  
• However, decisive technical information is missing: hepatic segments involved, relationship to major vessels or biliary structures, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio are all listed as “Missing” in the analysis. Without knowing whether an adequate FLR can be left (≥20 % of healthy liver, ≥30 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) the surgeon cannot confirm that a curative R0 hepatectomy is feasible.  
• In addition, the status of the primary rectal tumor (resected or not) is “Missing,” which influences the sequencing of surgery (primary‑first, liver‑first, or simultaneous).  
Because a specific prerequisite (assessment of FLR and vascular anatomy) and clarification of primary‑tumor status are required before a definitive operative plan, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging and molecular work‑up  
   – Obtain a thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain) – currently “Missing.”  
   – Perform full molecular profiling of the rectal primary (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) – currently “Missing.” This will guide the choice of targeted agents in subsequent systemic therapy.  

2. Rectal primary management  
   – If the primary tumor has not yet been resected, plan neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (long‑course CRT or short‑course RT followed by consolidation chemotherapy) as recommended for locally advanced rectal cancer, then reassess for TME (low anterior resection vs. APR) after systemic therapy.  

3. Systemic therapy continuation / conversion  
   – Continue or intensify systemic therapy to maximize tumor shrinkage. Options include:  
        • Continue FOLFOXIRI if tolerated, or  
        • Switch to FOLFIRI + anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab) if RAS wild‑type, or  
        • Add anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) if RAS‑mutated, based on molecular results.  
   – Aim for further downsizing of the residual liver lesions and monitor CEA trend (baseline 1200 ng/mL, decrease not reported).  

4. Restaging of liver disease  
   – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and perform volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
   – Assess vascular contact/invasion and biliary involvement (currently “Missing”).  

5. Decision on hepatic resection  
   – If FLR ≥20‑30 % and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection: proceed to curative liver surgery.  
        • For bilobar disease, consider a staged approach (portal vein embolization (PVE) or two‑stage hepatectomy) if FLR is borderline.  
        • If lesions are limited to segments that can be resected while preserving at least two contiguous segments, a single‑stage major or extended hepatectomy may be performed.  
   – If FLR insufficient: perform PVE (or ALPPS in selected high‑volume centers) to induce hypertrophy, then re‑resect.  

6. Sequencing of surgeries  
   – Liver‑first strategy is preferred when the primary is asymptomatic and liver disease is the dominant threat, provided the patient’s performance status is adequate.  
   – Simultaneous resection can be considered only if the hepatic resection is limited (≤2‑3 segments) and the primary can be safely removed in the same operation.  
   – Primary‑first is indicated if the rectal tumor causes symptoms (obstruction, bleeding) or if the rectal margin is at risk; after TME, reassess liver for resection.  

7. Post‑operative/adjuvant therapy  
   – After hepatic resection (and/or primary resection), resume systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± targeted agent) for 3‑6 months as adjuvant treatment, guided by pathological response and molecular profile.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – determines technical feasibility of hepatic resection.  
• Detailed hepatic anatomy: segments involved, vascular/biliary contact – essential for planning resection type or need for PVE/ALPPS.  
• Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected or not) – dictates sequencing of surgeries.  
• Comprehensive staging for extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) – rules out contraindicating metastases.  
• Molecular phenotype of the primary tumor – influences choice of targeted systemic agents and overall prognosis.  
• Maximum and minimum lesion diameters – help in volumetric calculations and assessment of response.  

Acquiring these pieces of information will allow conversion of the “Potentially resectable” classification to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
- Completeness: Both recommendations cover the major clinical domains concerning management of patients with primary colorectal tumor and liver metastases. Both address resectability assessment, preoperative imaging and restaging, systemic therapy options, surgical planning, and consideration of postoperative therapy. There are no significant differences in these areas, so the completeness criterion is satisfied.

- Step Concordance: Both recommendations classify the case as potentially resectable and highlight the need for detailed imaging and evaluation to confirm resectability. They both propose a sequence involving further imaging, systemic therapy continuation, and eventual surgical re-evaluation. Therefore, they are step-by-step concordant.

- Case Tailoring: Recommendation 1 includes specific molecular profiling for the primary tumor to guide systemic therapy and discusses the sequencing of surgeries based on the rectal primary status. Recommendation 2 mentions multiple advanced techniques like intra-operative ultrasound and parenchymal-sparing strategies without explicitly discussing the molecular profile or specific sequencing of surgeries related to the rectal primary. There are differences in case-specific details like the use of minimally invasive approaches and intraoperative techniques, which shows a lack of case-tailoring concordance.

- Missing Data Concordance: Both recommendations highlight the need for FLR estimation, detailed hepatic anatomy, segmental distribution of lesions, and status of the primary tumor. They both mention the importance of advanced imaging and molecular profiling, although with slight variations in specifics like liquid biopsy in Recommendation 2. Overall, they identify core missing data similarly.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver MRI shows three residual lesions < 2 cm after a major chemotherapy response, which from an oncologic viewpoint suggests that complete (R0) removal is feasible. However, decisive technical information is missing: the exact hepatic segments involved, relationship to major vessels or biliary structures, and, critically, the future liver remnant (FLR) volume needed to ensure postoperative liver function. In addition, the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease has not been documented (no thoraco‑abdominal CT or PET‑CT reported). Because these missing data directly determine whether a safe, curative hepatectomy can be performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Complete restaging  
   - Perform a thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases (addresses the “Extrahepatic Metastases” missing items).  
   - Obtain a high‑resolution pelvic MRI and/or endoscopic evaluation of the rectal primary to determine its current T‑stage, depth of response, and need for further local therapy.  

2. Functional and volumetric liver assessment  
   - Calculate FLR using CT‑volumetry or MRI‑based software; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in a healthy liver), plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment the remnant.  

3. Multidisciplinary decision  
   - If no extra‑hepatic disease and FLR is adequate (or can be made adequate), schedule curative‑intent liver surgery.  
   - Preferred hepatic approach: parenchyma‑sparing non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmentectomies of the three lesions, preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage (technical criteria from the literature).  

4. Management of the rectal primary  
   - If the primary has not yet been resected and imaging shows no threatening circumferential margin, proceed with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) or total‑neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) as indicated, followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) 6–8 weeks after completion of CRT.  
   - If the primary is already resected (to be confirmed), no further local therapy is needed.  

5. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Given the excellent biochemical response (CEA ↓ 1100 → 80 ng/mL) and RAS‑wild‑type status, continue peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) for 2–3 months after liver resection, then resume or complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy.  

6. Adjuvant considerations  
   - Discuss the role of postoperative hepatic ablation (RFA/SBRT) for any marginal residual disease that may be unresectable intra‑operatively.  
   - Institute standard postoperative surveillance (CEA, cross‑sectional imaging every 3–6 months).  

Step 3 – Missing data that are most crucial for the recommendation  

- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume – required to confirm technical feasibility of hepatectomy.  
- Exact hepatic segment location and vascular/biliary involvement of the three residual lesions – determines whether a parenchyma‑sparing resection is possible without vascular reconstruction.  
- Status of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET, peritoneal assessment) – any distant metastasis would shift the strategy toward systemic therapy or combined approaches.  
- Current status of the rectal primary (resected or not, symptomatology, need for CRT/TNT) – influences timing of colorectal surgery relative to liver surgery.  
- Baseline liver function and performance status – to assess operative risk and need for pre‑habilitation.  

Acquiring these pieces of information will allow conversion from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive “Resectable upfront” plan and guide the precise surgical sequence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
**Completeness:**
Both recommendations cover similar clinical domains: liver metastases resectability, preoperative imaging, systemic therapy, surgical approach, and postoperative management. They both emphasize the need for comprehensive restaging, liver volume calculations, integration with the management of the rectal primary tumor, and postoperative therapy.

**Step-by-step concordance:**
The recommendations differ significantly in how they assess resectability. Recommendation 1 classifies the case as "potentially resectable" pending further assessment, while Recommendation 2 considers it "resectable" with conditions. Their management steps diverge: Recommendation 1 follows a structured oncological strategy with sequential assessments and interventions, while Recommendation 2 focuses on a comprehensive re-evaluation of all metastatic sites with a detailed plan based on a disease map.

**Case-tailoring concordance:**
Recommendation 1 and 2 differ in the inclusion of certain patient-specific details: Recommendation 1 emphasizes RAS-wild-type status and the need for peri-operative chemotherapy, while Recommendation 2 includes additional molecular insights like MSS/MSI status and liquid biopsies. These differences reflect distinct approaches to case-specific tailoring.

**Missing data concordance:**
Both recommendations recognize the need for detailed segmental and volumetric data of liver lesions. However, Recommendation 2 uniquely highlights the importance of molecular characteristics and liquid biopsies, which Recommendation 1 does not address. Therefore, they do not align in the identification of missing data required for further planning.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Current imaging shows 7 viable liver lesions (6 stable, 1 progressing 5 cm in segment VII) after systemic therapy, but key anatomic and functional data are missing (vascular contact, biliary involvement, future liver remnant volume).  
- One lesion is progressing, indicating that disease control is not yet achieved; further downsizing or local control is required before a curative‑intent hepatectomy.  
- Missing staging of the chest (no thoraco‑CT) and lack of liver MRI prevent definitive assessment of extra‑hepatic disease and precise hepatic anatomy.  
- Primary colorectal tumor status (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding) is unknown, which influences sequencing of surgery.  
Because a specific prerequisite (complete thoraco‑abdominal staging and additional systemic or locoregional therapy to control the progressing lesion) is required, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain a thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
   - Perform a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to define lesion number, size, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
2. Assess the primary tumor  
   - Determine whether the left‑colon primary has been resected; if not, evaluate for obstruction, perforation or bleeding.  
   - If the primary is still in situ and symptomatic, plan primary resection first (or simultaneous resection if the hepatic procedure will be limited).  
3. Systemic therapy  
   - Continue the current oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., mFOLFOX + bevacizumab) for up to 2–3 additional cycles, aiming for further tumor shrinkage.  
   - If the segment VII lesion continues to progress, switch to second‑line therapy (e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) as per conversion‑therapy protocols described in the literature.  
4. Local control of the progressing lesion  
   - Consider image‑guided ablative therapy (microwave or radiofrequency ablation) or stereotactic body radiotherapy for the 5 cm segment VII metastasis if it remains unresectable after systemic therapy.  
   - If the lesion becomes resectable and FLR is adequate, plan a curative‑intent hepatic resection (potentially a right posterior sectionectomy or extended hepatectomy).  
5. Re‑assessment of resectability  
   - Repeat liver MRI and CT at 8–12 weeks after the additional systemic/locoregional treatment.  
   - Calculate FLR; aim for ≥30 % of total liver volume (≥40 % if prior chemotherapy).  
   - If all lesions are controlled and an R0 resection is technically feasible, schedule hepatic resection.  
6. Surgical sequencing  
   - If the primary tumor is still present and requires resection, decide between simultaneous (if hepatic resection is limited) or staged (primary first, then liver) based on operative risk and extent of liver surgery.  
7. Adjuvant therapy  
   - After curative hepatectomy (and primary resection if not already performed), give 6 months of postoperative chemotherapy using the same regimen that achieved disease control, per standard conversion‑therapy protocols.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast for precise lesion mapping, vascular/biliary involvement, and FLR calculation.  
- Future liver remnant volume assessment (FLR ratio).  
- Status of the colorectal primary (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstructive/bleeding symptoms).  
- Details of vascular contact or invasion by the hepatic lesions.  
- Current CEA level and trend (to help gauge treatment response).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations differ significantly in terms of completeness, step-by-step concordance, case-tailoring, and missing data concordance.

1. **Completeness:** Recommendation 1 considers the case as potentially resectable, with a detailed multi-step plan for both further staging, systemic therapy, and possible surgical interventions. It includes specific steps for imaging, assessing the primary tumor, and local control strategies. Recommendation 2 considers the case as unresectable, focusing on systemic therapy adaptation, detailed restaging, and considers local treatment only if systemic control is regained, suggesting cytoreduction as a goal rather than resection. The approach to adjuvant therapy and postoperative considerations differ significantly, indicating a lack of completeness alignment.

2. **Step Concordance:** In Step 1, there is a fundamental difference in the resectability assessment: Recommendation 1 considers the disease potentially resectable, whereas Recommendation 2 assesses it as unresectable at the current stage. In Step 2, Recommendation 1 proposes a structured sequence including imaging, systemic therapy, and surgery contingent on response, while Recommendation 2 focuses on systemic therapy adaptation and considers local treatments only conditionally. This discrepancy in the approach indicates a lack of concordance.

3. **Case Tailoring:** Recommendation 2 provides additional details on molecular profiling (MSS/MSI, mutation status), which are not addressed explicitly in Recommendation 1. Furthermore, the recommendations differ in their consideration of the patient's performance status and specific approaches to integration of systemic and local therapies, reflecting different levels of tailoring to case specifics.

4. **Missing Data Concordance:** Both recommendations require imaging for future liver remnant estimation and primary tumor status. However, Recommendation 2 includes additional missing data such as molecular profiling and ctDNA/CTCs, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. This indicates a lack of concordance in identifying essential missing data.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The thoraco‑abdominal CT shows a radiological complete response of the bilobar liver metastases after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing. Specifically, a liver‑specific MRI (to exclude occult residual disease and to assess vascular anatomy) and an evaluation of the rectal primary (MRI pelvis and endoscopic assessment) are absent. Without these data the safety of an upfront liver resection or a simultaneous primary‑tumor operation cannot be determined, therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending the prerequisite investigations.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to verify true complete response, delineate any residual lesions, and define vascular and biliary anatomy.  
• Perform a dedicated rectal work‑up: pelvic MRI and flexible sigmoidoscopy (or proctoscopy) to assess for clinical complete response, residual tumor, or ulceration.  
• Review pathology (if any) of the primary tumor to determine whether it has already been resected; if not, plan definitive local therapy based on the rectal assessment:  
   – If a clinical complete response is documented, consider a non‑operative “watch‑and‑wait” approach with intensive surveillance (clinical exam, endoscopy, MRI every 3 months for the first 2 years).  
   – If residual disease is present, schedule total mesorectal excision (TME) after an appropriate interval (4–6 weeks) from the last chemotherapy dose.  
• Based on the liver MRI findings:  
   – If no viable disease is identified, forego hepatic resection and continue observation; maintain surveillance with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the abdomen every 3–6 months.  
   – If residual lesions are detected, plan curative‑intent liver surgery (single‑stage or two‑stage depending on distribution) ensuring an adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % in a normal liver). If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
• Systemic therapy: Given the radiological complete response and normal CEA, discontinue further chemotherapy unless disease recurrence is documented; resume systemic treatment only if progression occurs.  
• Multidisciplinary follow‑up: Continue MDT review every 2–3 months to integrate imaging, endoscopic, and laboratory data and to adjust the plan promptly.

Step 3 - Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Liver MRI (presence, results, vascular/biliary involvement).  
• Status of the rectal primary tumor (has it been resected? current imaging/endoscopic findings).  
• Molecular phenotype of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide any further systemic considerations.  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
• Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and exact number/size of lesions before treatment.  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio calculation.  
• Assessment for brain metastasis (MRI brain).  
These items directly influence the decision to proceed with hepatic resection, the need for primary‑tumor surgery, and the overall oncologic management plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment

MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of IVC invasion (>1 cm) makes an R0 hepatic resection technically demanding and requires either vascular reconstruction or down‑staging of the lesion. In addition, key information needed to confirm feasibility (future liver remnant volume, chest/abdominal staging for extra‑hepatic disease, and status of the primary colon tumor) is missing. Therefore resection cannot be performed upfront and must be preceded by systemic therapy and further imaging assessment.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or FOLFOX/FOLFIRI + anti‑EGFR agent given RAS‑wild‑type left‑sided primary) to assess tumor biology and attempt downsizing of the IVC‑invasive metastasis.  
- Obtain complete staging: contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, nodal or osseous metastases; repeat liver MRI with vascular phase to delineate the extent of IVC involvement and arterial/portal anatomy.  
- After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, restage with imaging; if the IVC‑contact lesion has responded (reduction in circumferential involvement) and no new extra‑hepatic disease is identified, proceed to functional assessment of the future liver remnant (CT volumetry).  
- If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy; reassess FLR 2–4 weeks later.  
- Surgical plan (liver‑first approach):  
  • Perform an extended right hepatectomy or right trisectionectomy encompassing segment VII lesion, with en‑bloc resection of the involved IVC segment and reconstruction using a prosthetic graft or autologous vein, in collaboration with a vascular surgeon.  
  • Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- After hepatic recovery (≈4–6 weeks), address the primary left‑colon tumor: either simultaneous colectomy if operative risk acceptable, or staged segmental colectomy (primary‑first or primary‑later) depending on patient fitness and intra‑operative findings.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6–8 cycles, adapting regimen based on response and tolerability.  
- Enroll patient in regular surveillance (CEA, imaging every 3–6 months) and consider multidisciplinary review for any recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Primary tumor status (resected or not) and histologic grade – essential to decide timing of colon resection.  
- Exact size of each liver metastasis and total tumor burden – influences FLR calculation and surgical planning.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume or ratio – determines need for PVE or two‑stage approach.  
- Comprehensive thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT or PET‑CT) – to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy of the liver – required for safe vascular control and reconstruction.  
- CA 19‑9 level and other prognostic biomarkers – may affect classification as borderline resectable.  
- Current systemic therapy exposure and response – needed to gauge biological aggressiveness and suitability for down‑staging.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships on liver MRI : precise extent and depth of IVC invasion
B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for intensive chemotherapy and for potential major liver surgery including complex vascular surgery.
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
I. a chest CT scan
Reasoning:
**Completeness:** Both recommendations cover similar domains in terms of resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative considerations. They both discuss the need for systemic therapy prior to surgery, complex resection strategies involving IVC reconstruction, and considerations for the primary tumor and subsequent surveillance. Therefore, they are aligned on completeness.

**Step-by-step Concordance:** Both recommendations classify the case as potentially resectable, contingent on downsizing and thorough assessment, involving systemic therapy and restaging to assess response before considering surgery. The proposed management steps are consistent in terms of the sequence: systemic therapy, imaging guidance, and surgical planning involving a complex resection strategy if feasible, followed by management of the primary tumor. Thus, they align in step concordance.

**Case-tailoring Concordance:** Recommendation 1 is more detailed in discussing the sequence of surgical interventions (liver-first approach, specific surgical techniques), whereas Recommendation 2 focuses more on the potential for minimally invasive surgery and the use of prehabilitation and ERAS protocols. Recommendation 2 also includes details about molecular profiling (BRAF, RAS status) and specific systemic therapy choices tailored to RAS wild-type, which are not elaborated in identical depth in Recommendation 1. Additionally, Recommendation 2 mentions prehabilitation and ERAS protocols, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. These differences indicate a lack of case-specific tailoring concordance.

**Missing Data Concordance:** Recommendation 1 is more focused on missing data for liver surgery planning (e.g., FLR volume, arterial and portal anatomy), while Recommendation 2 highlights several unique missing data points such as the molecular profile of the primary tumor (MSS/MSI) and systemic findings such as liquid biopsies (ctDNA, CTCs), patient’s performance status, and tolerance for chemotherapy. These differences indicate a lack of concordance in the identification of missing data.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the case lacks decisive technical information (hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary contact, future liver remnant volume) and the primary colon tumor has not yet been resected. Because these missing data directly affect whether an R0 liver resection can be achieved, and because down‑staging with systemic therapy is usually required for six lesions of 2–4 cm, the disease cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Begin with systemic conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status; aim for 3–4 months (≈6 cycles) to assess tumor biology and achieve possible downsizing of liver lesions.  
- Simultaneously evaluate the primary tumor: if asymptomatic, the primary can be resected after systemic therapy; if any obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms develop, address surgically or with endoscopic stenting before or during the liver operation.  
- Restage after chemotherapy with high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary‑specific contrast) and repeat CT to define:  
  • Number and distribution of lesions across hepatic segments,  
  • Vascular and biliary involvement,  
  • Calculation of FLR ratio (target ≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % if steatosis or prior chemotherapy).  
- If FLR is insufficient but disease has responded, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (initial limited resection or ablation → hypertrophy → completion hepatectomy).  
- When imaging confirms that all liver disease can be removed with negative margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments, plan curative‑intent surgery:  
  • Option A: simultaneous resection of the primary colon tumor (left‑sided colectomy) and a single‑stage major hepatectomy if FLR permits.  
  • Option B: staged approach – first colon resection, then liver surgery after recovery and confirmation of disease control.  
- Aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions; intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult disease and guide additional ablation if needed.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen as used pre‑operatively) for 6 months, unless contraindicated.  
- Follow‑up with serial CEA, imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months; monitor circulating tumor cells as a prognostic adjunct.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most critical for decision‑making)  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (prognostic impact).  
- Confirmation whether the primary colon cancer has already been resected.  
- Presence of obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms from the primary.  
- Exact hepatic segment distribution of the six metastases.  
- Presence or absence of vascular, biliary, or portal vein invasion.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio.  
- Liver MRI results (necessary for precise mapping and detection of additional lesions).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to guide sequencing of primary‑tumor versus liver surgery.  
- Prior systemic therapy details (if any) and response assessment.  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases (2–4 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Despite the bilobar distribution, the number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The detection of circulating tumor cells reflects increased systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Mandatory peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resections of all six lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
E. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
F. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.
